cited_evidence.text: A commonly adopted strategy to overcome this strength-ductility tradeoff is to develop multi-phase microstructures, involving at least one ductile/soft and one hard/strong phase, mixed in the appropriate proportion. Common examples include duplex alloys, such as 2205 stainless steel, which have a hard bcc phase to increase the strength of the alloy and a soft fcc phase to maintain the tensile ductility while deformation. The goal has been on fine-tuning the alloy composition and/or processing conditions in order to obtain a material with a good balance between ductility and strength. Eutectic alloys, often exhibiting a two-phase lamellar microstructure, offer such a possibility, and have been investigated for many years in different classes of alloys. Eutectic morphologies are characterized by the simultaneous growth of two (or more) phases from the liquid. A recently developed new class of eutectic HEAs (EHEAs), have attracted a lot of attention due to their promising mechanical properties. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.

Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials. decision.trend: The trend in the research on eutectic high-entropy alloys is to improve their strength and ductility simultaneously. Earlier studies focused on designing new alloys with specific compositions and microstructures, such as the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy, which showed a good combination of strength and ductility. Later studies explored various processing techniques, including cryo-rolling, annealing, and hybrid-rolling, to further enhance the mechanical properties of these alloys. The use of phase-selective recrystallization and nanostructuring with structural-compositional dual heterogeneities have also been investigated to achieve ultra-high strength and ductility.
decision.unsolved: Despite the progress made, the simultaneous improvement of strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys remains a challenge. The current research has not yet fully addressed the issue of achieving ultra-high strength and ductility in these alloys, and further studies are needed to explore new processing techniques and alloy designs.
decision.why: The next step in the research on eutectic high-entropy alloys could be to further explore the use of phase-selective recrystallization to achieve ultra-high strength and ductility. This technique has shown promise in recent studies, and its combination with other processing techniques, such as nanostructuring and thermal or thermomechanical treatment, could lead to the development of new alloys with unprecedented mechanical properties. The use of phase-selective recrystallization could allow for the creation of alloys with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in a hard phase, leading to improved strength and ductility.
